flawed_step: Step 3: inserting v into the Hamiltonian cycle C of G−v needs v to be adjacent to two vertices that are next to each other on C, and the hypothesis does not guarantee this.
counterexample: Petersen graph (outer 5-cycle 0-1-2-3-4, spokes i-i', inner pentagram i'-(i+2)'). It is connected with 10 vertices and is not Hamiltonian: a Hamiltonian cycle of a cubic graph on an even number of vertices would give a 3-edge-colouring, but its chromatic index is 4. It is vertex-transitive, and P−0' has the Hamiltonian cycle 0-1-1'-3'-3-2-2'-4'-4-0, so every P−v is Hamiltonian.
assessment_summary: Proof attempt: (1) Fix v; by hypothesis G−v has a Hamiltonian cycle C on n−1 ≥ 3 vertices. Justified by the hypothesis. (2) G is connected, so v has a neighbour u_i, which lies on C. Justified. (3) Replace the edge u_i u_{i+1} with u_i v u_{i+1} to get a Hamiltonian cycle of G. NOT justified: this needs v adjacent to both u_i and u_{i+1}, which nothing guarantees. (4) Choose a different v or C until the insertion works. NOT justified: nothing forces such a choice to exist, and hypohamiltonian graphs exist. (5) Conclude G is Hamiltonian. NOT justified, since it depends on steps 3 and 4. The statement is false: the Petersen graph is non-Hamiltonian (chromatic index 4), yet P−v is Hamiltonian for every v. By vertex-transitivity one check suffices: P−0' has the cycle 0-1-1'-3'-3-2-2'-4'-4-0, and all its edges are verified.
